subject_entity.notes: Tertullian's anti-Jewish treatise (c. 198–208); argues that Christ's dominion has reached nations beyond Roman access including Britannia; contains an early rhetorical claim of universal Christian spread.

object_entity.notes: First major Latin Christian author; active in Carthage c. 195–220. Wrote at least 31 works spanning apologetics, anti-heretical polemic, and moral discipline. Coined 'trinitas' and 'tres personae una substantia'. Defender of apostolic succession, rule of faith, incarnation, and bodily resurrection. Later attracted to Montanist rigorism c. 207; teacher of Cyprian by doctrinal influence.

context_place.notes: Major North African city; center of Latin Christianity from Tertullian through Cyprian and Augustine; seat of important regional councils.

subject_entity.notes: Hippolytus's treatise against the modalist Noetus of Smyrna, c. 200–210; defends the distinction of Father and Son against Patripassianism; affirms the Logos as a distinct divine person who became incarnate; important pre-Nicene trinitarian witness.

object_entity.notes: Roman presbyter and theologian; prolific Greek-speaking writer in Rome; opposed the modalism of Zephyrinus and Callistus; set himself up as rival bishop c. 217 (sometimes called the first antipope); exiled with Pontian to Sardinia in 235; reconciled before death; author of the Apostolic Tradition, Refutation of All Heresies, Against Noetus, and Commentary on Daniel.

evidence.notes: Scholarly attribution based on style and theological consistency with other Hippolytan works.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Some introduce among us a certain Noetus of Smyrna, who taught that Christ himself was the Father, and that the Father himself was born and suffered and died. They say: Christ was himself the Father and the Father himself suffered.
passage.notes: Introduction of Noetus's modalism/Patripassianism: Father = Son = Christ who suffered

source.title: Against Noetus
source.author: Hippolytus of Rome
source.notes: Anti-modalist treatise defending distinction of Father and Son; ANF Vol. 5 translation.
